utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-84-T, the Prosecutor versus Ramush Haradinaj et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. I think that the witness can be brought into the courtroom. Meanwhile, Mr. Di Fazio, I think the re-arranged exhibits for Witness Andjelkovic were expected yesterday, I think, and at quarter to 7.00 in the evening, nothing had been received yet. MR. DI FAZIO: Well, yes, I realise -- sorry, I didn't realise that, Your Honour, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that you'll look after the matter. MR. DI FAZIO: I'll take care of it and make sure --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's good. MR. DI FAZIO: -- that the matter is attended to today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: Your Honours, in the meantime, I just wanted to inform you that there are some photographs that the Prosecution has obtained and provided hard copy to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: And electronic copies are being provided to the Defence as well, and we also have a set of hard copies for the Trial Chamber, three, which are available for you to look at, if you wish. They were obtained by Barney Kelly, one of our investigators, and he has been ill and only came in yesterday following his mission. And I only became aware of them last night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we'll see the photographs, and we'll hear whether there's any problem with the source of the photographs, yes or no. Mr. Emmerson, I take it that you're ready to continue your cross-examination, but I'll first tell the witness -- yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just before Your Honour does, there is one matter I wanted to bring to Your Honour's attention in relation to a different photographic exhibit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- arising from Your Honour's questions yesterday afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I have no objection to the witness having his earphones on, but it is a matter which touches upon locations in evidence. I have provided to the usher three hard copy photographs and to the Prosecution. Your Honour asked for a marking of where Smajl Haradinaj's house is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can I just orientate Your Honours on this particular photograph?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: On the bottom of the photograph Your Honours can see just about the centre of the page, that is working from left to right but at the bottom, the Haradinaj compound. Does Your Honour have that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, bottom of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, you put it like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Right, yes. Yes, that's clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And so Your Honours can see the road --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- up towards the main road into Gllogjan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And then the dog's leg to the right into the village --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's perfectly clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think the photo that Your Honours have and we were looking at yesterday afternoon was probably taken from an aerial position roughly above the blue circle looking --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, as a matter of fact, I have reasons to believe - but we'll check that - that the portion and with a blue circle is, as a matter of fact, on one of the photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's -- because from what I remember it is, but at least now we know -- I take it, Mr. Di Fazio, that if you would disagree with this location of the -- of Smajl's house, that we'll hear from you. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Emmerson, having dealt with this. Mr. Stojanovic, the Chamber meanwhile received photos on which it can identify where exactly Smajl's house was, so you don't have to bother about that anymore. Mr. Stojanovic, I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you gave at the beginning of your testimony, and Mr. Emmerson will now continue his cross-examination. Please proceed, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. I wonder if we could have Exhibit Rule 65 ter number 1146 back up on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We still need to assign a number to that -- no, we have done that already. Then perhaps you can refer to it as -- I think it is D28 -- D29.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, have you had an opportunity to think overnight about whether, in fact, you were interviewed by a lady from the Humanitarian Law Centre on the 25th of April?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And having reflected on it, do you now accept that you were, in fact, interviewed by that lady on that date?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, but I don't think so. I don't think I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very well. Well, we have, as I indicated to you yesterday, a record from that lady, who's given evidence about having interviewed you and recorded what you said. And the statement that we're all looking at contains an account which follows in most details or many details the account which you have given us in evidence and is written as though it were your words. So I'm going to ask you just one or two questions about it, and we can consider the question of how it came to be made separately. I put to you yesterday afternoon that there was no mention in that statement of Daut Haradinaj having entered your house with the men you say came in first on the 18th of April. Do you recall now whether you mentioned Daut Haradinaj at all to anyone at around this time as having been present?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think -- or at least, or rather, I'm sure that in the first interview I gave to "Illustrojana Politika," I did mention this.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: But you've seen that interview, Mr. Stojanovic. Your words are recorded in detail and in quotations, and though names are mentioned, there is no mention of Daut Haradinaj having been present?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I was able to see yesterday, the interview - it's been a long time - this interview was not published in its entirety at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The record of the interview between you and the lady from the Humanitarian Law Centre ends with the following words which I'm going to read to you. "90 per cent of them," that is the men who had been involved in this incident, "90 per cent of them were in uniform and had small arms. They took their masks off. None of them kept his mask on. They were mostly my neighbours, guys I went to school with, kept company with, shopped in their stores, so I know 95 per cent of them. The remaining 5 per cent I didn't recognise because they weren't from our parts. I guess they were from villages further away." Now, does that accurately record or reflect -- does that accurately reflect your recollection, that all of the people concerned at one time or another took their masks off and that you knew 95 per cent of them or recognised them by sight, and that the other 5 per cent were people who must have been from some other parts?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, because I said I knew 90 to 95 per cent of those people, I probably meant, or rather, this means that I actually recognised Daut Haradinaj. And as for the 5 per cent, there were some people that I just didn't know and -- or perhaps they were just younger than I was and that was the reason why I didn't know them.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You see, on the first page of this document, the front sheet, there is space in which the names of any perpetrator which has been provided by the witness is recorded under the heading "Perpetrator Information" -- "Perpetrator Identification Information," and there are two names recorded as having been provided by you; the first is Nasim Haradinaj and the second is Zed or Ziqi Nimonaj?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zeqir Nimonaj. I do apologise, I put this name first because he was the one trying to calm the situation down, but at the same time he was also making gestures, indicating that they should continue to beat us. I also mentioned this name because he was there in the room where we were beaten in Smajl Haradinaj's house. So these two persons were specifically relevant for me personally in that time, in that case, and that is why I mentioned their names, I specified their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And you remember that, do you now, specifying their names to this lady and not the names of other people?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall this lady. I already said that I couldn't remember this lady or giving an interview to her. I can, in fact, vouch for the fact that I was never interviewed by her.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just bear with me for one moment, please. Let me move on then, please, to the statement that you made to the Prosecution in this case on the 1st of November, 2001. I just want to be clear, Mr. Stojanovic. Had you made previous witness statements to the police about this incident?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never gave any statements to the police. I never had any contacts with the police. Do you -- just a moment. Let me get this straight. After I left or after I was released or before that?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: After the incident occurred, after you were released on the 18th of April, at any time did you make a statement to the police, a written statement, to the police?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so, but I don't really recall this.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You see, we have the copy of the statement that you made to the Prosecution in this case in November 2001, and in that statement you do mention Daut Haradinaj as having been amongst the men who entered your house on the 18th of April. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So I'm going to suggest to you that that was the first time you had mentioned in any statement to anybody the suggestion that Daut Haradinaj entered the property with those men.

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you that you are making a claim, and I am making a counter-claim. I am saying something that is opposite what you say. The first time that I mentioned those names was to this journalist from "Illustrojana Politika."

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: One or two things, please, about the statement that you made to the Prosecution in November 2001. First of all, you described Besnik Haradinaj, the person who was interrogating you in the small room of the house, as being 16 to 17 years old. That was what you said in your witness statement. Is that correct? Was he 16 or 17 years old?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how old he was. I gave an estimate, and I learned from Dragoslav that his name was Besnik. I knew that he was Rasim Haradinaj's son.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Leaving the name aside then for a moment, the person who was asking you questions in the room, did he look to you to be about 16 or 17?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, that's what he looked to me, perhaps even younger or maybe older, but that was the impression that I got.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You also said in your statement - and I'm reading a passage to you now - you said, describing those who were at Smajl Haradinaj's house, you said: "Many of the soldiers were children, 11, 12, 13 years old." Again, is that correct, that statement that you made to the Prosecution, that many of the people you saw and described as soldiers were children?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. On some occasions, I was guarded by children with weapons in their hands. They were standing opposite the three of us after we were thrown out of the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Did you know by this stage, Mr. Stojanovic, that three teenagers from the village had been shot and killed on the 24th of March by Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I already said yesterday, this is what I read in "Zeri Rinisi" and "Rilindja" one day after the incident, that is on the 25th.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So these children that you saw during the day, did any of them say anything to indicate to you that their classmates, their friends from the village, had been shot on the 24th of March?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Mention was made in the room, but not during the time that they guarded us.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So that was mentioned to you during the questioning by the 16- or 17-year-old boy who had you in the room, was it?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You said the death of the teenagers was mentioned to you while you were in the room being questioned, I thought. And a few moments ago, you told us -- a few moments ago, you told us that the person asking you questions was a 16- or a 17-year-old boy. Was it him who mentioned to you that teenagers from the village had been killed?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I didn't say that he told us that, but Zeqir, while he was there, he mentioned that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can I just get the picture of what was happening a little earlier on while you were being walked through the village. Is it right that people were coming out of their houses and hitting you and your brother and cousin, people from the village?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. To be quite specific, as I said yesterday, people came out of Xhavit Nimonaj's house or people would come from the meadows, out of the houses in Glodjane.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Was it your impression that really the whole village was turning on you?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, you told us yesterday, in answer to Mr. Di Fazio, that you were accused during this - you and your family - of having spied for the Serb forces before the 24th of March?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, that's not what I said. I didn't say that it was my family, but what I said is that when Zeqir Nimonaj was beating us, this is the context, I said that Zeqir Nimonaj said that I was a spy.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Did any of the other people who came out of their houses in the village, did they accuse you of spying as they were coming up to you or say anything that suggested that they thought that you and your family were responsible for what happened on the 24th of March?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I want to move on just to one other matter, please, arising out of the statement that you made. I just want to ask you a little bit about the condition of your brother Dragoslav at various stages in the proceedings. You've told us already that when you went or were taken to Smajl Haradinaj's house, Dragoslav was taken first into the small room, leaving you and Veselin in the corridor outside. And you've described to us a moment when Dragoslav was taken out of the room and put back in the corridor. Now, in your witness statement, I'm just going to read to you what you wrote, you wrote this: "They opened the door after interrogating him," that is Dragoslav, "and threw him into the corridor and he was unconscious. He was bloody and looked very bad." Is that -- is that a fair description, was he unconscious, as you said in your statement?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes -- well, he was not fully conscious.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: That's what I just wanted to clarify with you. I want to ask you for a moment about the period of time between the moment when he came out of the room and the moment when you were taken in, because I think you told us that Veselin was taken into the room first after that and you were left alone with your brother for a time. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I can't really tell you how long it took because I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I understand that, but I think you can give us an idea, can't you, how long Veselin was in the room alone before you were taken in?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I can't. I really don't remember how long it lasted, because at that time I hardly thought about things like time, the passage of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: In your witness statement, you said it was half an hour between Veselin going into the room and you being taken into the room. Does that sound right to you?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may have said this, or rather, I'm sure that I did say that, but whether this was, in fact, the length of time, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, leaving the length of time aside, I just want to ask you, during that period of time, however long it was, a little bit more about the state of your brother Dragoslav. Did you try to talk to him?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tried to talk to him. He could barely nod and squeeze my hand. So when I said that he was not fully conscious, he could just -- he could not talk at all. We could communicate just by gestures or he would make some facial expressions. And then one of the soldiers guarding us would approach me and would warn me against helping him or would even beat me up for helping him.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just concentrating on him for a moment, was he able to recognise your voice? Did he know it was you?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm sure he was able to recognise me because he squeezed my hand at one point. He wanted to tell me something by that, but he just didn't have enough strength.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You said in your statement he was bloody. Was there blood on his face?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And you were sure he recognised you because he squeezed your hand. Was he looking into your face?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure, 100 per cent. He couldn't look me in the face because he was all curled up.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So he couldn't look you in the face because he was all curled up. Can you just describe that in a bit more detail for us, please?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he was on the floor curled up, that was the position in which he was. He perhaps was able to glance at me, but that was not much. And I tried to get from him -- I was asking him, Where does it hurt? And so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And he was in such a bad state, he couldn't answer you?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he couldn't answer me.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Then you've told us you were taken into the room, and you've described what happened to you and Veselin inside. You then came out again, and I'm just going to read to you a passage from the statement you made in November in 2001. You said: "After two hours, we were ordered by Besnik to get dressed, and Veselin and I were thrown into the hallway corridor, and I saw Dragoslav on the floor unconscious." Pausing there for a moment, that two-hour period, is that also something we should take with caution because you're not sure about the length of time?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my statement I said around two, but it may have been mis-recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No, I'm not criticising you at all for this. I'm just clarifying with you, Mr. Stojanovic. Could it have been a much shorter period of time than two hours?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So what is the shortest period of time it might have been?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly not under two hours. They made me translate a piece from the "Politika" magazine. I probably forgot to mention that in my statement. So that took a long while, too, most probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Is that the piece we've looked at? No, it can't have been that piece. What was the piece from the magazine they were asking you to translate? It may be that there's no translation of that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you hear the last question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please answer it.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: What was the magazine article about from "Politika"?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The article was about the doctor and his team, that was two weeks before. He went to the village of Glodjane to administer some vaccine to some children there, but he was pulled over and detained. So that was about that particular incident and the person in question is Dr. Mirko Pesic.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very well. There may be some other information about that incident, so I'll come back to it in another part of the case. Let me ask you this: When you came out again after that interval, was Dragoslav - as you said in your statement - was he still unconscious on the floor?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And by that stage, was he in the same condition as you had last seen him?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was even worse.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: By that stage he'd lost consciousness fully, had he?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not fully, but it was getting worse. It probably hurt more and the internal bleeding had already increased in all likelihood. He was vomiting blood by this time. All of which led me to conclude that his condition had deteriorated.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. And then after a time, you were taken outside and taken off to repair your Lada. That was the next stage in the process. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes -- no. Now Nasim Haradinaj came, telling us that we would be released.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Meanwhile, some other things had happened, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, just let's be clear about this. You said in your statement it was about 3.00 that Nasim came and told you you were going to be released?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Then you said he offered Dragoslav a pill for the pain; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And then he said somebody needed to come back with him to search the house, and you volunteered. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. It wasn't like that. It's true that Nasim gave Dragoslav the pill. Dragoslav then came to. Later on Nasim told me that we would be released and that one of the cars would be returned to us. One of us, the three of us who were there, were to come with him and get the car. I knew immediately that he was talking about the Lada.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Let me just read to you what your statement says so that we're clear and check whether you agree with it? You said this: "It was about 3.00 p.m. and Haradinaj Nasim, son of Smajl, came and said that they will be released later with a car and someone needed to go with them to search the house. Nasim even gave Dragoslav a pill for the pain. I volunteered. I saw the time on the Albanian watches, so I knew it was 3.00. We walked back towards the village, and Nasim asked me where we would like to be released. I told him Babaloc." So just so that we're clear it was about 3.00 that Nasim arrived. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And it was very shortly after that that you were told that you were going to be released. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was before that. It was on his way in that he told us that we would be released and that he would return one of the cars to us, so it was before 3.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: But he arrived at 3.00 you told us. The time is less important than the sequence, Mr. Stojanovic. The question I'm trying to get clear with you is this: It was when -- it was when --

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. Nasim is arriving, he tells us about Dragoslav, and then we're off. Nasim, I, and a third person who was with us, and we are now heading for the car. So that's your sequence.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Prior to the arrival of Nasim, had you seen Hilmi?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the yard with Ramush, as I said before -- no, no, no, not before. My apologies, not before. It was once we were out that door that we laid eyes on Nasim.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Let's just get this right. It was once you came out that door that you laid eyes on Hilmi; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: That's what I just wanted to clarify with you. So you saw Hilmi Haradinaj there for the first time at the moment you'd been told you were being released?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. That wasn't the first time. I believe I said yesterday, Hilmi at one point on that day came while Dragoslav was still unconscious. He gave him some fruit juice or whatever it's called. I can't be very specific about the time-line, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You see, what I wanted to suggest to you, Mr. Stojanovic, is that it was the arrival of Hilmi Haradinaj that resulted in you being told you were going to be released?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Do you know how long before you were told by Nasim that you were going to be released. Do you know how long before that, it was that you first saw Hilmi?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be very specific, but I think it only took a very short while.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So he was on the scene a very short time before you were told you were going to be released. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember now.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So when the head of the Haradinaj household arrived, you were released?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not when he arrived. It was Nasim who told us that we'd be released. I don't know who took the actual decision to release us.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us that you went to the house, your house, and you then came back to the KLA HQ, as you described it, Smajl Haradinaj's house, and you went back upstairs and you then found your brother Dragoslav in the guest-room. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first thing I said may have been mis-recorded, but I said that in all of my statements, virtually. We were on our way to the house, but we didn't actually reach the house. We reached the house -- we reached the road forking off towards Hilmi Haradinaj's house, and that was where I found the Lada.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you. I'm simply asking you about your brother Dragoslav and his condition when you came back. When you came back, you told us you saw him in the guest-room. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, in your statement you said this, you said that you could see that Dragoslav was conscious at times and fainting again, and that his head was full of blood when you saw him there. Can I be clear, when you saw Dragoslav in the guest-room on your return, was he still drifting in and out of consciousness?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I want to move on now to another topic. I'm conscious of the time. I shan't be a great deal with this, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I want to move to another topic, if I can with you briefly, and that is the 24th of March. You arrived that day, you told us, in -- to your house having travelled from the direction of Dubrava village. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And you told us that police were in Dubrava and that you'd had to ask them to get through. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, have you heard ever of a Serbian general who was in the area called General Bozidar Delic? Is that a name you've ever heard?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The only reference I came across was the evidence here in The Hague, but back in the area I'd never heard that name. I did move about a lot, and I did know quite a few Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just to be clear, you just said a moment ago the only time you'd ever heard his name was in connection with the evidence here in The Hague. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, the evidence, the Milosevic evidence. That was the first reference to him I'd ever heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: That's what I just wanted to ask you about, Mr. Stojanovic. In the Milosevic case, General Delic gave evidence that there were 400 Serbian security forces stationed in the village of Dubrava conducting a blockade on the 24th of March. I'll put that to you again, the evidence that General Delic gave in the Milosevic case was that on the day you passed through Dubrava and had to ask for permission, there were 400 Serbian security forces in Dubrava. I want to ask you, please, to tell us what you saw of police, army, and security services in the area as you were approaching towards your house?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Except for those two who allowed me to get through and the one I saw at Glodjane, I don't know. As for Delic's comments, I don't know, it's difficult for me to comment on his statement, and I think you should probably ask him. The 20 -- I saw some along the road and some on the property.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You're misunderstanding my question, I think. I'm not asking you about the police you saw who were in the area around your house. I'm asking you about the presence of police before you got to your house. You told us that you were stopped in Dubrava.

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two who stopped me in Dubrava. They were securing the area - how should I put it? - in order to stop anyone from just heading there for no reason at all and get themselves killed. They stopped me, and then I asked them to let me through since my house was across that -- behind that line.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Perhaps we can put it a different way. What about when you left that evening, did you see large numbers of Serb troops in the area or Serb police?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see. Armoured vehicles, did you see what sort of vehicles the police --

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: All the police officers in the area around your house, Mr. Stojanovic, presumably they had arrived in vehicles. Did you see the vehicles, marked vehicles?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did see vehicles such as Pinzgauers, but no armoured vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see. So you saw Pinzgauers, roughly how many?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two or three, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And were you aware that a large number of people from the village had been detained by the police on the 24th of March?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You see, I want to suggest to you that quite a large number of people were arrested and that evening collected in the front yard around your house by the police?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's what I said in my statement. Had somebody been brought into the yard or in front of the yard, because it was prior to that that we had spoken to the policemen telling them not to bring anyone into our yard at all. I'm not sure if they complied or not, but I spent 80 per cent of that entire time inside the house, especially that evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And just be clear, why were you telling the police not to bring people into your yard?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were our neighbours, after all, so we knew how people related to one another. We knew what exactly went on, those people they were fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Why did you tell the police that you didn't want them to bring those people into your yard?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told them those were our neighbours. It was for that reason and all the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Do you know Shaban Zeqiri? Shaban Seqiri?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Shaban, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: He's an elderly gentleman, isn't he, who used to be in the police and lived in Glodjane?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he used to work with my brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You see, Mr. Stojanovic, did you come to learn that Shaban Zeqiri was amongst a number of people arrested and beaten by the Serb police that day from the village?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Did you ever see Shaban Zeqiri again after the 24th of March?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. That evening, as I said, we had to leave the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You mentioned helicopters. Were you able to see from inside the house what the helicopters were doing?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So you had a clear view from inside the house of that, did you?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not as they were just flying around, but when they got near the house and when they flew around the house, yes, I did have a clear view.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And was there a lot of shooting going on at that time?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean a lot of shooting? By the helicopters or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The question I'm asking you is: Whilst the helicopters were there, was there a lot of shooting generally going on at that time?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a distant sound of shooting, not really nearby.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Weren't the helicopters there at the time that the shooting was taking place between your property and the Haradinaj property?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember if the helicopters were there at that precise time, but I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You mentioned a period of time when there was shooting going on between your property and the Haradinaj property, and you told us in your evidence in answer to Mr. Di Fazio that there came a point where the fighting moved down towards Gllogjan. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I want to suggest to you that immediately before the fighting moved down to Gllogjan, the helicopters were hovering above the Haradinaj compound and firing at it.

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I categorically claim -- well, perhaps not categorically. What I'm saying is that I didn't personally hear any of the helicopters open fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Would you be able to recognise the difference --

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At one point in time, one of the helicopters was parked on Ibrahim Maloku's meadow just outside my house. As far as I knew, they were waiting for a chance to evacuate Otovic who had been injured, but he later succumbed to the wounds he received.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Two final questions, if I may. First of all, you've told us that your brother Dragoslav was there during the day. We have seen a witness statement or a witness interview record with your brother Vladimir, who says that he was there also during the day. Was Vladimir there during the day?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vladimir was called by the mother. His youngest son, 3 years old, was in our home, and his mother was afraid and she called him over that afternoon sometime.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So is the answer yes, that during the day he was, in fact, there?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not during the day, that afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: All right. And finally this: Could you please be shown Exhibit D19?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: For the witness, we will need the Serbian -- that's it. Can we go, please, to page -- the fifth page of that document. And for Your Honours, it's the sixth page of the English version, so the sixth page, because the first page is a declaration. Could you read for us, please, the words that appear at the top there in that heading. Do you see the central word there beginning with a letter "C," could you read everything that is in that heading for us, please.

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The Republic of Serbia, the Ministry of Internal Affairs, Secretariat of Internal Affairs, Djakovica police station."

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, and then the heading in the centre of the page, please?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "List. "Members of the PJP of the Djakovica SUP variant for daily allowance payment period between 23rd of March and 31st of March, 1999."

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can you tell us who the person at number 2 on that list is?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you just tell me what "PJP" means, please, and about Predrag Stojanovic, that's what it says, "Predrag Stojanovic." What is a member of the PJP?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, it's not, I'm afraid, Mr. Stojanovic, for me to give evidence about that. You're tell us that you don't know?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And did you know that Predrag was in the paramilitary police, at least in 1999?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know he was with the regular police forces. I know nothing about any paramilitary police. I know that he was a beat officer. That's as long as we're talking about my own Predrag, my brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can we just look down, please, to number 17. Who is that?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My brother is called Veselin Stojanovic, but he had been working for 25 years as a private entrepreneur in Indjija. I state categorically that he never had any sort of police or military involvement anywhere at all. As for this Veselin Stojanovic, I don't know. Perhaps you should go and have a look at other lists, too. There is no father's name stated here next to Predrag's name or Veselin's for that matter. Predrag Stojanovic and Veselin Stojanovic, Mijat Stojanovic, those are exceptionally common names in Serbia. It's difficult for me to try and shed any light on this unless their fathers' names are actually included.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You can shed some light on it, Mr. Stojanovic, because you've just given us some evidence that I want to clarify with you. Is it, as you've just told us, your evidence that your brother Veselin is somebody about whom you can categorically state he was never in any way in the police? Is that a categorical statement that you are giving this Tribunal on oath?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 100 per cent certain. The five years -- over the five years preceding this he had not been to Kosovo at all. He had never been to Kosovo until we were arrested, even after our release. These names mean nothing to me without the father's name. Veselin owns a shop in Indjija and had owned that same shop for over 25 years. You can go to any institution in Serbia and they will most certainly confirm that for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, may I draw your attention to the fact that the witness introduces a time-frame --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, exactly, I was just about to ask that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You've just indicated that your brother Veselin did not arrive back in Kosovo until after you were arrested. When was that that he arrived back?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not for five years, the five years before the war, not before and not after. That's what I meant --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well when --

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, when did he come back to Kosovo, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see. So he never came back during the war?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not during the war and not after.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see. I just want to ask you this:

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Could we please look at Defence document identification 1D020739, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, that would be number ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Exhibit Number D30, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, this is a note made by Mr. Di Fazio, the gentleman who sits ore there and who asked you some questions earlier about a meeting he had with you on the 23rd of March, that's four days ago, in The Hague in which he asked you some further questions about your evidence. Do you remember meeting Mr. Di Fazio?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can you have a look, please, at the second page of this document and at the penultimate paragraph beginning: "Occupations ..." I'm going to read this to you slowly in English so that you can have it translated to you. The note that Mr. Di Fazio made of your conversations reads as follows: "Occupations - witness," that is you, "was in the paint business, Dragoslav was a care-taker in a school in Decane and Veselin worked in a furniture company in Decane." Now, why would you be telling Mr. Di Fazio that Veselin worked in a furniture company in Decane and now be telling this Tribunal that he hadn't been in Kosovo before or during the war, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me make this clear, this is Veselin Stijovic, not Stojanovic. He was with us when we were captured. So this is the point. This is not Veselin Stojanovic, my brother, but this is my cousin or a relative of mine; in other words, Veselin Stijovic and Veselin Stijovic did work in Sipad.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see. And so the following sentence where you say this: "Neither I nor my brother were mobilised into the police or the army in 1998, and I don't know about Veselin." Are we to take that as a reference to Veselin Stijovic as well?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: As far as you were aware, was Veselin Stijovic involved in the police?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Veselin Stijovic, I know for sure, we were in the camp up there, I know that he never worked in the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see. So if that's right, just to be clear so that we know --

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can you explain --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, and I'm also looking at Mr. Di Fazio, may I take it that: "Neither I nor my brother were not mobilised," is a mistake; that it is: "Neither I nor my brother were mobilised."

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: That's how I'd read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Di Fazio, is that a correct reading? It's not a double negative, it's a single negative? MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, okay, understood. Please proceed, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: When you told us just a moment ago that you are categorically certain that Veselin Stijovic never worked for the police, can you help us as to why you said to Mr. Di Fazio, I don't know about Veselin?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if, in 1998, he was engaged in the military, or rather, 1999. I think that the question related to his involvement in the military or whether he had a rifle. As far as I can remember, this is what we were talking about. But I can tell you that he did not, he was not, because we were in the camp, he was never in the police. I never saw him wearing a police uniform, and in those bungalows where we lived ...

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the position of you, Mr. Guy-Smith, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It remains the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And the same would be true for you, Mr. Harvey?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And for me, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, is there any reason for you to re-examine the witness? MR. DI FAZIO: Just a few minor matters, if Your Honours please. I can wrap it quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Re-examination by Mr. Di Fazio:

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier being made to translate a "Politika" magazine, and as I understood your evidence that had -- that occurred sometime after being beaten and tortured in the Smajl Haradinaj's house. Firstly, is that where you were required to translate the "Politika" magazine?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Were you asked to do that by one of your captors; and if so, can you recall which one?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The man whose name I don't know who went with me to get the Lada, and throughout this period I was able to observe that his command of Serbo-Croat was very good, and I started translating. It was a short article, maybe just half a page.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: All right. But they asked you to do that; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Because he was monitoring me as I translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you also said - just bear with me and I'll find it from the evidence - you were asked by Mr. Emmerson about police bringing people into your yard. Now, you were asked -- well, in fact, it was suggested to you that there were a large number of people who were arrested and that evening collected in the front yard around your house. And you had spoken to police, telling them not to bring anyone into your yard at all. Firstly, did the police bring arrested persons into your yard, as far as you're aware, on that day?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, no, but because my house is right there at the roadside, perhaps what they meant was this yard.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but it's just not getting any clearer, and I want to be as clear as possible. First of all, did you, with your own two eyes, see - see - any arrested people in your yard at all?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Did you, with your own two ears, hear any information to the effect that people had been -- arrested people had been taken into your yard; and if so, from whom did you hear that?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never heard any, up until this moment now.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson asked you this question and you gave this answer: "Q. Why did you tell the police that you didn't want them to bring these people into your yard?" And you answered: "I told them those were our neighbours."

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: "It was," unfortunately a word is missing, it was something to do with "reason and all the rest." Now, did you ever tell the police --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: The witness said "it was without reason." MR. DI FAZIO: Oh, I see. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: We've just had an explanation. Your answer was this: "I told them those were our neighbours. It was without reason and all the rest." Did you ever speak to the police about not bringing people into your yard?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At one point during the day, yes, with the police officer that stood on the road in front of the house, although at that time there was no discussion about -- no mention was made of any captives or prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: What did you have in mind -- what was troubling you about people being brought into the yard? What was your concern?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I lived in that area. We had lived with these people, and I didn't want to see anyone. All the more so -- in fact, let me explain. This is a very uncomfortable situation. I simply didn't want anyone to put me in an uncomfortable situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Okay. And how long does it take to walk from your place into the -- say, to Smajl Haradinaj's house?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it all depends on how fast you're walking, but it's a kilometre, kilometre and a half. So it should take you about 15 minutes if you walk at a normal pace.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Has the re-examination triggered any need to --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just one matter, if I might.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Further cross-examination by Mr. Emmerson:

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, you've just been asked questions by Mr. Di Fazio about people in your yard and looking at the transcript at page 29, line 25, Mr. Di Fazio asked you this: "Firstly, did the police bring arrested persons into your yard, as far as you're aware, on that day?" And you replied: "As far as I know, no, but because my house is right there at the roadside, perhaps that's what they meant was this yard." What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said perhaps that's what they meant since a car was close -- parked close to the yard. So one of those Pinzgauers that I mentioned was parked close to the yard on the road. Perhaps that's what they meant when they referred to the yard, and that's why I said it.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, perhaps that's what who meant?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I, that's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Who was referring to people being by the Pinzgauer parked outside your house? Who was referring to detained people being by --

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody mentioned it, but I said during the day when we talked, I said to the police officer, Please do not put me in an uncomfortable situation. Please do not bring people to my yard. So if there were any prisoners or captives, because we had to think about all the aspects of the situation, lest we should be put in an uncomfortable situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: What would -- what gave you the idea in the first place that the police might be planning to bring arrested people into your yard so that you had to raise it with them?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, because police had come from this direction, the police that I had seen, and we know that in every ...

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, we lost the end of your answer. Let me ask you the question again. You say that police had come from this direction, which direction?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of the police that I saw came from this direction, and as soon as I saw three Pinzgauers, two or three Pinzgauers, I assumed that they had come from this direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: From which direction?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the direction of Dubrava.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So you saw them and they were outside your house, were they? Parked on the road outside your house?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One Pinzgauer was parked on the road next to the house, quite near to the house. It was not at the entrance gate or right at the house, very near the house, but it was close enough on the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So just finally, you told us just a few moments ago that you, seeing that Pinzgauer, you asked the police not to bring people into your yard, and I asked you the question: What gave you the idea in the first place that they might be planning to bring arrested people into your yard so that there was a need to tell them not to? And you said: Well, because police had come from this direction. Can you just explain to us, just explain to us why it was you thought that the police may be intending to bring people to your yard, of all places?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't explain to you why it was that I thought so at the time. It was a long time ago, but I thought -- in fact, out of an abundance of caution, I didn't want anyone to get arrested or captured. But I simply didn't want us, me, to be put in an uncomfortable, unpleasant situation. This was the reason, because after all we were the ones living there.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And simply this: Do I understand your evidence correctly, is it that you were concerned that the people in the village would think your house was being used effectively as a military facility. Is that what you were worried about?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would have one additional question in relation to this same matter, Mr. Stojanovic. Earlier you were asked why you were telling the police not to bring people into your yard, and then you said: Those were our neighbours. Did you have any clue as to who would be the arrested persons at that time?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I assumed, I really didn't know, but I assumed that the people who had been firing on the police, that they could perhaps get arrested or captured.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that is a reference to the Haradinaj -- members of the Haradinaj family or at least those who were living on the Haradinaj property?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't mean anyone specific. I didn't mean Haradinaj specifically or anyone else, but because there had been fighting I actually had in mind the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that answer. Any further questions? If not, Mr. Stojanovic, this concludes your testimony in this court. I'd like to thank you for having come to The Hague and to have answered questions of the parties and of the Bench. You are excused, and I wish you a safe trip home again. Madam Usher, would you please escort Mr. Stojanovic out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for calling me here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I suggest, since we really need our time today that we leave -- I don't think that there are any major problems with exhibits, but let's not spend time on it at this very moment. Let's just continue. Therefore, Madam Usher -- she left the courtroom meanwhile. Mr. Di Fazio, are you ready to call your next witness? MR. DI FAZIO: Mr. Kearney is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kearney. MR. DI FAZIO: And if Your Honours please, I might excuse myself briefly and I can inform the usher myself that the next witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if you do that, that might save time and at the same time if the new photograph which is not yet in evidence, but if that really would depict where Smajl's house was located, it couldn't come as a surprise that on P32 the witness -- the other Stojanovic witness was not able to identify the house because it's not on the picture. We spent approximately two pages of transcript on producing the picture, asking questions whether he could orient himself. I have had more moments when I was impressed by the efficiency of the examining party. If I read the transcript, I might have misspoken if I said I have had more moments when I was impressed. I meant to say, I have had moments when I was more impressed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kearney, no protective measures for the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And your next witness is ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Mr. Veselin Stijovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, Mr. Stijovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require that you make a solemn declaration that you speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is now handed out to you by Madam Usher. I would like to invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Stijovic. Please be seated. You'll first be examined by Mr. Kearney, who's counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Mr. Stijovic, good morning --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kearney, I take it that for the scheduling of Thursday that you're fully informed about that if we can't conclude the testimony of this witness today, that we have to sit tomorrow even if it would only be for half an hour. The witness has been scheduled for one hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am aware of that. Your Honours -- obviously this morning's session went longer than we all thought it would, so I'm going to do my best to stream-line these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Mr. Stijovic, good morning. Could you again, please, state your full name for the record and give us your date of birth, as well as your place of birth?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Veselin Stijovic, and I was born in Decani in 1972.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: What is your father's name, sir, and your ethnicity, if you could tell us, please?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: I am a Serb and my father's name is Bogic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Mr. Stijovic, you mentioned that you were born in the village of Dasinovac. How long did you live there after your birth place?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Dasinovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kearney, I see in the transcript, and that's what I heard translated, that the witness was born in Decani, and that of course could be municipality or city, but until now I have not heard Dasinovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: I'll clear that up, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Mr. Stijovic, were you born in Decani itself or in a village in the Decani municipality?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: I was born in the hospital in Decani, but I lived in the village of Dasinovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: How long did you live in that village, please?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: From the day I was born.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: As of 1997, could you tell us, please, what the ethnic break-down was in the village of Dasinovac?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: There were Albanians, Catholics, and Serbs. There were about five or six Catholic houses, about 50 Albanian houses, and about ten Serb houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Stijovic, given that you lived in Dasinovac all your life, I assume you went to school there, and you had interactions with your neighbours throughout the course of your lifetime. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I went to school in Donji Ratis, elementary school, I mean, and I had dealings with all my neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Now, just in a general sense, we'll talk about this more specifically later, but in a general sense before 1997 how would you characterise your own relations with your Albanian neighbours, please?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Before 1997, I had good relations with them; we were on good terms. I socialised with my neighbours, Albanians, Serbs, and Catholics alike. I was on good terms with all of them. We went to school together.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Now, in just a moment we're going to talk about events that took place in late 1997 and 1998, but before that I need to talk with you briefly about your employment history. Tell us, please, today how you're employed, first of all?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: I am a construction machinery operator now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: During the course of your employment career, did you ever work for the VJ, please?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Were you ever in the army, sir?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: I was in the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: What dates were you in the army?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: After you got out of the army in 1992, what was your occupation then?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: I got a job in a furniture factory in Decani.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: How long did you hold that job in the furniture factory in Decani?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: From 1992 until 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: When, in 1998, did you stop working at that furniture factory?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: I stopped working there when I was captured.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And we'll talk about that in a moment, but, sir, at the time of your capture would you characterise your employment as civilian or military?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: I worked as a civilian, as a craftsman, in the furniture factory. What I did there was manufacture beds and stuff like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned earlier that before 1997, the relations between yourself and the Albanians in your own village of Dasinovac was good. At some point in 1997 or 1998, did that begin to change, Mr. Stijovic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kearney, I'm looking at the clock, and I'm listening to your question. You're entering a new area, I take it. Therefore, I think it's better to have a break now. I have one question for -- to the Defence teams. Listening to the last ten minutes of testimony, would there have been any objection if Mr. Kearney would just have put for confirmation to the witness where he was born, where he went to school, whether he was working here, et cetera, et cetera? Mr. Kearney, that saves you approximately half of the time. I take it -- I see nodding no.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Clearly, there's one area of employment which I would have thought it was perfectly respectable for Mr. Kearney to elicit without leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: In other words, excluding certain possibilities. I had indicated to Mr. Kearney yesterday afternoon the nature of the areas which have been in dispute with the last two witnesses and what is not in dispute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And, therefore, quite large parts of the evidence-in-chief could be taken reasonably shortly, but it's obviously up to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I noticed that the Prosecution until now has never used 89(F). I mean, all these questions are put to witnesses and, of course, we get answers to those questions, but the question is whether the efficiency would not be served by trying to find ways of speeding up in those areas which are not in dispute. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I hope the Chamber has noted that I have specifically been refraining from making a number of objections --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, yes, you see --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- the past couple of days. That was because of this very reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, it's a standing objection. We have that not only in the back of our mind but even in the front of our mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And just to be entirely fair to the Prosecution, I think on one occasion when Mr. Dutertre was examining, he did lead the witness on those personal details at the outset and simply invited the witness to confirm without objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let's not have a debate on it. I think the message is clear enough, if we can find means to save time without in any way jeopardising the information the Chamber receives, it should be -- it should be given a try. We adjourn until five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kearney, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you. At the outset, I would like to inform the Trial Chamber that I did speak with Mr. Re over the break. He did hear the Court's concerns about using 89(F) more, and he wanted to convey to the Trial Chambers that it's our intent over the break to begin that work in earnest for using both 89(F) and 92 ter to stream-line the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Mr. Stijovic, when we left off, I was just asking you if at some point, in late 1997 or 1998, the relations between Serbs and Albanians in your village of Dasinovac changed. Can you please tell us, one, if that's true; and two, if it is true, how?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: It is true that there had been a change in the tensions between us, and then the attack occurred on Malesa Culafic's house. I read about that in the papers and I personally went there the next day because those were friends. We were on visiting terms. I just went there to see if they could use any help or anything. After that, there was the attack on the police station in Rznici - I read about that, I saw it on TV - and the murder of Otovic. Dragoslav and Mijat told me they had had to leave their home that night for reasons of personal safety. It was often the case that people would pass by houses at night firing shots, so eventually for safety reasons I, too, had to leave the house in which we lived. And, eventually, I had to go to Decani.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: When you say for reasons of safety you had to leave your house, please tell us about that. What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, to keep the same thing from happening to my family that had happened to Malesa Culafic, and in order to keep my family safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: When was it, Mr. Stijovic, that you left your village?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: I can't be specific about the date, but it was sometime in April, late March/early April.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier in your testimony Dragoslav and Mijat. Let me ask you: Do you have two cousins who go by those names?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, two cousins, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And those cousins lived in the village of Dubrava. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And at some point during this same period, were you aware that they also left their home in Dubrava for Decani?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they told me they had been forced to leave for reasons of safety at about the same time that the police officer Otovic was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Beyond your cousins and your own family, were you aware that other Serbs were leaving Dasinovac at that time, at that general time-period, as well?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, at that general time-period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Now, at some point after both you and your cousins left your respective homes, did you travel back to Dubrava with your cousins to help them at their home?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They had asked me to come and give them a hand, get some things for them, things for their livestock and all the basic necessities. We drove there in a Lada and in a Mazda 626. We started loading things into the cars, and then suddenly an attack started. We dashed into the house, and the attack itself went on for about 45 minutes. They were firing, using automatic weapons and hand-held launchers. Mijat and I stood in a corner of one of the rooms, we took cover there, and Dragoslav would nip over to the window every now and then to see if they were approaching the house or getting any closer. And then he would tell us what he had seen outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Do you remember what date that was, sir?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: It was a Saturday, just the day before Easter, and I can't remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: This was a day in April of 1998, though. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: You said that after this attack started you ran into your cousins' home. At that point did you actually see who was firing on the home or did you find that out later on?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: It was later on that we found out. It was from Glodjane and from all directions. It was difficult for me to tell where the fire was coming from. About 45 minutes later they finally reached the house and they started shouting for us to come out and surrender. Dragoslav was the first to the door and was followed by Mijat and me. They told us to lie face-down. Dragoslav was the one who opened the door. They started beating him first and then later came up to us two and beat us and kicked us and hit us with rifle-butts and with whatever they could use, whatever was at hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: After which they threw us out of the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: I just want to go back for a moment. You said they were firing hand-held launchers on your home. Did you actually -- how did you know that? What did you see or what did you hear in that regard?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: It was because of the powerful detonations that we could tell.
