Those were powerful explosions as they impacted against the house, and Dragoslav was actually watching through the window. And later on we saw it ourselves once we were outside. I saw people carrying hand-held launchers around.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: How many of these explosions did you hear as they impacted the house?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly how many, but quite many. We were quite scared, traumatised, so I didn't keep track exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: You said the attack lasted for approximately 40 to 45 minutes. How many rounds of rifle fire or gun-fire hit the house during that period if you can tell us, please?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: The firing was constant, uninterrupted, but I can't tell you about the number of rounds. It went on like that for 45 minutes non-stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: During that attack, Mr. Stijovic, did either you or either of your cousins fire back at the people who were attacking you?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: No, we had nothing to fire with, no weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: You said at some point earlier in your testimony that the shooting came to an end and words were yelled from outside toward you. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Once they reached the house they stopped firing and they shouted for us to come out. Dragoslav opened the door and Kika and I were ordered inside the house to lie down on the floor and keep our heads down and not look around. About 30 soldiers came running into the house. Dragoslav was hit as soon as he opened the door, and then later they came inside to beat the two of us as well with automatic weapons and whatever else they could use.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Do you remember what it was exactly that these men were yelling at you at that time?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: They shouted abuse, very bad things. They referred to our Serb mothers, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: What language were they yelling in?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: These 30 soldiers who came running into your house, please describe them for us?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Describe, some were -- all were armed, some in uniform, some in civilian clothes, all armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: They were in uniform of what organisation?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Camouflage uniform; just whose make I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Did you see insignia on the uniform, sir?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Please describe it for us and tell us what the insignia was?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: There was a red circle and a black eagle with, I think, yellow lettering, but I'm not sure about that, if it was yellow or not, but it said "Kosovo Liberation Army."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: You said that as they came in they attacked Dragoslav. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Describe that attack for us, please?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: As soon as he opened the door, they started hitting him with automatic rifles in the stomach, in the head, indiscriminately. They were just hitting away, five, six, or even ten of them all at the same time, and he had fallen down to the floor. They told us to lie down even before they got to us, and when they got to us there were three of them, and they started hitting away with automatic weapons, their rifle-butts, that sort of thing. They took us outside the house. Again, we were told to lie down, face-down, and not look away, and not look at them either. And they continued to beat us for a while, after which they told us to stand up and they took us to Glodjane. We stood up, and they took us down that road to Glodjane. There were many armed soldiers and civilians lining that road --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Mr. Stijovic --

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: -- beating us all the while.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: -- I'm going to stop you for a moment, please. I want to talk just for a moment about the blows that you suffered during this attack. You indicated that after the men came into the home, you were told to lie down. Were you yourself beaten during that period while you were still inside the home; and if you were, tell us how many times you were beaten and where on your body, please?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Mijat and me, they beat us many times. They kicked us and hit us with automatic weapons. They hit us in the house for quite some time, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Where on your body were you hit?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: On my head, my body, my -- indiscriminately. They weren't very picky. They were just hitting away.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And did this -- did this beating continue after you were taken outside of the home; and if it did, please tell us again the number of blows, the duration, where on your body the blows landed?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Outside the house, there was the same situation replayed as the one inside the house. They told us to lie face-down, and they kicked us and hit us with automatic weapons all over, on our heads and our bodies. They didn't mind, five, six, or even ten of them, as many could get close to our bodies on the ground, they all tried to get in a blow or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And what were you doing during this time?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: We were just lying on the ground, trying to protect our heads with our hands to the extent that we could.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: During this beating, this second beating if you will, the one that occurred outside of the home, were the men talking to you or talking to any of you during that time that you heard?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: For the most part, they were abusing us. They were cursing. I didn't really understand every single thing they were saying in Albanian, but I did get the gist of it, the abuse and everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Do you speak some Albanian, Mr. Stijovic?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And when you say you got the gist of it, what gist did you receive? What did you hear them saying to you?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, abuse. What are you doing here? This is our land. They called us Chetniks, that sort of thing. They abused us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: When you say they said to you, This is our land, what specifically did they say and what did you take that to mean, please?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what they meant exactly when they said, This is our land. I can hardly be expected to explain what they were trying to say or, for that matter, the hatred that they turned on us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Had you ever met, to your knowledge, any of these men before, Mr. Stijovic?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Not those who were outside the house with us, but by the time we were taken to Glodjane, the HQ or whatever it was, I was able to recognise some people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And we'll talk about that in just a moment, but I want to focus now on the men beating you in the courtyard. You said that they -- you talked about the fact that they focused their hatred on you. What was the basis of their hatred?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: I really can't explain, just because we were Serbs. I don't think there could have been any other reason. I had never clashed with any of them or Mijat for that matter, not that I know of.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Mr. Stijovic, do you remember making a statement to ICTY investigators back in 2002 about this incident?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And Court and counsel, I'm referring now to a statement on page 4 of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Did you tell the ICTY investigators back in 2002 that you heard these men say: "Kosovo belonged to the Albanians." First of all, do you remember making that statement to the investigators; and secondly, is that true, did they say that to you?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's precisely what I meant, Kosovo belongs to us, it belongs to Albania. What are you doing here, what business have you being here, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Now, you mention at this point in the courtyard that you yourself did not recognise anyone. Did either of your cousins tell you that they did recognise somebody?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: They knew most of them, I think. I think they did. They told me that there was a man who at one point came to the yard and tried to defend us, tried to protect us from them. I think they said that this man was Nasim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And besides this gentleman named Nasim, did they tell you any other names of soldiers, of KLA soldiers, that they recognised?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Later on they told me about Zeqir, who beat us the most in that small room, the one who told us to strip to the waist and who beat us really severely. And I asked them, Who's that one? And they said, This is Zeqir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Mr. Stijovic, let's now get to that second location where you were beaten. You mentioned earlier in your testimony that at some point, you left your cousins' home in Dubrava and went towards Glodjane. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: How was it that you got there?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: We walked. They told us to put our hands in the air and keep our heads down and not look left or right. We passed a lot of their soldiers along the road, and everyone was hitting us on our way to Glodjane. Once there, they took us inside this house, where there were quite many soldiers. There was security outside the house in the yard. Some were cleaning their weapons, and some were just standing there. They took us into the house, up to the first floor, and left us in a corridor outside a small room where we sat down on the floor. After this, they took Dragoslav into that small room.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And let me stop you there again, if I may for a moment. You said that as you were walking along the road to Gllogjan, there were other soldiers along the way that beat you. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: As you were being beaten along that road, do you -- was anything further said to you by any of the men -- any of those men who were beating you?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Mostly they were shouting abuse at us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And when you say "abuse," again, please, just for the record, what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: They were cursing our Serb mother, all the things that I've told you about, what business had we being in Kosovo at all, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: These men that you passed along the road to Gllogjan, how were they dressed, please, and how were they armed, if you can tell us?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: They had automatic weapons. There were civilians and men in uniform, but all of them were armed. Some had military bottoms and civilian sweaters on top, and they were people who were fully kitted-out in military uniform, and they were civilians, too, who were carrying weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Did you again see the insignia of the KLA you described earlier worn by some of these soldiers?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: From the time you left the house in Dubrava until you arrived at the house in Gllogjan, how many KLA soldiers would you say you saw, sir?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: I can't say exactly, about a hundred I'd say, about a hundred soldiers, give or take a soldier or two but thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Now, before we start talking about what happened inside the house in Gllogjan, just tell us, if you could, what was your physical state as you were walking along the road toward the house. How were you feeling? Describe your injuries for us?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Dragoslav's condition was the most serious of all three of us. The two of us, the rest of us, were bleeding too and we were forced to walk with so much pain.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: On the way to Gllogjan, this is from your cousins' home to the second house you were taken, was Dragoslav able to walk along -- during that time?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: He was barely able to walk. We helped him along, but he progressed very slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: You said you were bleeding, Mr. Stijovic. Where were you bleeding from on your body, please?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: My head, my head for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: You told us you were taken to a specific home in Gllogjan. Describe the home for us, tell us what it was, if you know?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: It was a house just next to the road, the ground floor and the top floor. I think that side was -- or that's how I remember it. They took us into the house and left us in the corridor, after which they took Dragoslav into a room. It didn't take long, and by the time he was out of that room he was in a very serious condition. They threw him out and he fell down on the floor next to us and they took Mijat away and into that room. I tried to help Dragoslav. Somehow I heard that they were beating Mijat. They were beating him for some time, must have been for an hour or so. Mijat was then thrown out and I was called into the room. I walked into the room. There were two soldiers there, there was a table in the middle of that very small room and a chair as well as two soldiers, three sometimes. Other soldiers came in but two were a constant presence in that room and they were in charge of hitting and beating people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Let me stop you there, please, for a moment. Did you get an impression as to what this home was being used as, if you can tell us?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think it was their headquarters, command post of some sort, something like that, because the security was the heaviest there. Most of the soldiers were concentrated there in this place where we were taken to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: You said at some after you arrived, Dragoslav was taking -- taken into a room and yourself and Mijat stayed outside the room. Could you hear -- during that time-period, could you hear anything that was going on inside the room?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, while Dragoslav was in there, we heard some talking inside -- from inside the room, but when they opened the door and they threw him out he was already in a very poor shape because of the beating that he had sustained. And he could no longer take the beating. He started to lose consciousness. He was in severe pain, and I remember that Nasim brought some pills to him. He said, Take one of these, these are good for pain.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: How long was Dragoslav in the room before he was dumped back out in the outside area?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure, about half an hour, maybe more, maybe less, but something like half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: You said that when he was brought out he -- your words were: "He started to lose consciousness." I want to ask you: Did he lose consciousness? Were you able to talk to him during that period? Please give us more detail about that period?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: From time to time, yes, I was able to. He would come to for a little bit and then he -- the pain would come back and the pain was so severe that he would lose consciousness all the time. He drifted in and out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Were there times that he -- I want to ask you again, were there times that he -- when he drifted in from consciousness or when he was not unconscious, that you were able to talk to him during this period of time?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, no, no. Because even when he was conscious he was moaning and complaining about the pain -- well, we may have exchanged a word or two, but I can't remember now at this point because a lot of time has passed since then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: How long was Mijat kept inside the room, if you can tell us, and also could you hear anything that was going on when Mijat was taken inside the room?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I heard the blows, and I heard Mijat moan because of the blows. I don't know how long he was in there. I can't remember. I know that when he was thrown out, I was taken in, and then I was asked questions like, Do you have weapons? How many police are there in Decani? To my mind, these were just questions that gave them a pretext for them to beat us. They beat us anyway, but they used this information and those questions to -- as a pretext to beat us. So they beat me for about an hour, those two, all the time, and Zeqir was among them. And then he ordered me to take off my jacket and my shirt, because he thought that this bat or baton that he was using wasn't really inflicting all that much pain. And then he made me face the wall and to look at the corner, and then they used -- they -- actually, they beat me over my head and my back. And whoever got into the room beat me, too. And after a while they, brought Mijat back into the room, and Zeqir ordered him to strip to the waist. He did so, and then he went on to beat him. So then they beat both of us for a long time. I don't know how long it took, but it was a long time. And then they threw us out, and when they did so Dragoslav was in a very, very bad shape.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: All right. You've -- you've said quite a lot there. Let me catch up to you for a moment. You said that when you were taken inside the room, there was two men there. You identified one, I believe, as Zeqir. Do you know who the other one was that was inside the room?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't know these people, so that I can't tell you. I didn't know them. I was told about Zeqir by Mijat. Mijat told me, Zeqir is the one who beat us with this bat or baton. It had some kind of a spring wound around it, and there was a metal ball at the top, and this caused quite serious injuries. This lasted for a long time, and then we got out, and some people -- soldiers and some civilians, so some were wearing uniforms and some civilian clothes, they went in to get into the guest-room, which they call "sobura," and a man that I knew was among them, Deli Lekaj [Realtime transcript read in error "Jekaj"]. I knew him quite well. He had a hand-held launcher with him. He was in civilian clothes, but he had a grenade launcher, and he said, Well, why did you come here? And I said to him that I had come here to help my cousins. He told me, If they let you go alive, don't ever go back to Dasinovac because it's just a matter of time before we put a roadblock on the road leading to Dasinovac in the village of Pozar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: All right. Let me back up just for a moment. During the beating inside the room with this baton, how many times were you beaten with it if you can tell us, please?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, two or three hours. They beat us all the time without let, with the baton, with their fists, with rifle-butts. They really beat us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Can you describe for us the force of the blows that were landing on your body? If you can tell us anything about that, please.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he beat us with as much force as he had. He would, in fact, take a few steps back and then inflict the blow with this baton in order to make the blow as strong as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: This baton, describe it. How long was it? Can you show us with your hands?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kearney, do we really need these details? I mean, this is the third witness on the event. Do we have to know whether it was wood or plastic? I mean, the picture seems to be described in sufficient detail for the time being. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: I'll move on, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: You said that at some point, Mijat was brought into the room with you and the beating continued. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And after that, you were both thrown back outside the room. Is that true as well?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we were thrown out of the room to the place where Dragoslav was already down on the concrete floor, and he was in a very, very bad shape.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Describe Dragoslav's condition at that time for us, please. Was he -- first of all, what was his state of consciousness at that point?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: He was in severe pain. He was vomiting blood, and some soldiers would approach him and kick him and hit him, despite his condition, there in this corridor where we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Did you yourself recognise any of the soldiers that were beating him or kicking him at that point?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: You mentioned that it was during this time that you had the conversation with a gentleman you knew named Lekaj. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Deli Lekaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: How was it that you knew Mr. Lekaj?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I know him. I came to know him because he socialised with a relative of mine, so I got to know him through this relative, and we continued up to be on -- we were on good terms, and we went to Prizren to get some wheat there. He had a truck and he drove it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier that he was carrying a weapon. Was he dressed in military or civilian clothing at that time?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: He was in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: The men who were beating you inside the room, were they in military or civilian clothing?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: One had a regular military uniform, and the rest had uniforms -- civilian clothes, because some of -- they would come in and then go out. So all kinds of people wearing all kinds of clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier that when you spoke to Mr. Lekaj, he had words of advice for you. Is that correct? Please tell us again what they were, if you could.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. His advice to me was, If they let you go from here to go home. If they let you go alive, do not go to Dasinovac anymore, do not take the road leading to your house because it's just a matter of time before we go out and put a roadblock in at Pozar. And then you would be imprisoned again, maybe tortured, maybe something even worse than that. But at any rate, do not go back home.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Stijovic, that advice about the -- or that warning about the roadblock near Pozar, in your -- based on your own knowledge, did that -- at some point, did that prediction come true?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: When was that? Tell us about that.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know when it was that it came true, but I know that Stanisa Radosevic, Novak Stijovic, and Stanisa Radosevic's mother, they were, in fact, captured there in the village of Pozar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: At some point that day after the beatings, were you released?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Did they release us? Well, we were there in the corridor. They had the security guarding us. They took Mijat with them to fix the Lada. They said you should come with us and fix the Lada. Dragoslav and I remained there, and then we were taken out into the yard in front of the house to wash the blood off at a water-pump that was there, and he had to pump the water, even though he was in such a bad state, in order for me to be able to wash the blood off. And then I did the same for him. They forced us to clean off the blood that we were covered with on our heads and ears, and so on. Probably when they decided to let us go, but that was just before we set off for -- well, Mijat came back later on. He said that he couldn't fix the Lada. They then took us and ordered us to go back to Dubrava to their house. So we walked and then a tractor came by. And because Dragoslav was in such a bad shape, we put him in the tractor, and we slowly walked behind this tractor until we reached their house in Dubrava. Mijat was taken in front of the house --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Let me stop you there for a moment before we go back to Dubrava. You indicated at some point after Mijat went to fix the Lada, you and Dragoslav went out to the water-pump to clean your wounds. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they took us out to an area in front of the house for us to wash.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: When you -- you went from the corridor where you had been detained out to the water-pump, how did you get there? Did you -- did you and Dragoslav walk? Were you carried? Were you dragged? How did you get outside, please?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I helped Dragoslav to stand up. There was some soldiers guarding us there in the corridor, and they escorted us. It was very difficult. We could barely get down -- get him down, and even though he was in such a bad shape, they refused to use the pump, to help us pump the water, but we had to help each other do that, to wash off the blood. I assume that because they had decided to let us go, they didn't want us to be all bloody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: All right. Let me stop you there, Mr. Stijovic. My question simply is this: Did you -- you said you helped Dragoslav down towards the pump. Was he able to walk on his own a little bit, or did you have to physically carry him to the water-pump?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I had to carry him even though he was able to stand on his own two feet, but he was very shaky. So I didn't really carry him in my arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And even though he was shaking on his feet, it's your testimony that he was able to physically work the water-pump. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: He had to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Please tell us about the trip back to Dubrava. You indicated a tractor came, and Dragoslav was put on it and you walked. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, because he was in such a bad shape. They put him on a tractor -- in fact, we helped him climb up on the tractor, and we slowly walked behind him, Mijat and I, of course, and the soldiers that were escorting us and those that were standing by the road. When we reached their house, we stayed there at the very entrance into the yard. They took Mijat to a corner of the house. He had to remove the covers from a fruit tree of some sort that they had put there in order to protect it against the cold. Then they went into the house. They took some fabric, a sheet or something. They cut it into pieces and blindfolded us, tied our hands, put us in a car, and took us to the village of Babaloc, to an area close to the village of Babaloc. From time to time, they'd stop as we drove. I don't know whether there were any check-points there or just groups of soldiers. I don't know how that was organised, and these people would ask, Who are these people? Why are you letting them go? And their response was, These are good guys. We decided we'd let them go and so on. So that occurred at several places. So they took us -- it was in a red Opel Ascona car, that was the car that we were in and the car that they took us into Babaloc to an area close to the refugee camp. And then there they threw us out of the car and told us to look straight, not to look back, not to look to any side because otherwise they'd kill us. We walked slowly, and at one stage Dragoslav was unable to walk any further so I remained with him. I tried to help him move, albeit very slowly. And Mijat ran to the refugee camp and came back with a man who then drove us to the health centre in Decani, where we had our wounds bandaged and were sent to the hospital in Decani.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Let me stop you there --

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: The moment we got there Dragoslav --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Before we start to talk about the hospital in Decani, I want to back up for a moment, if I may. You mentioned earlier in your testimony that you -- from the trip to -- from Dubrava to an area near Babaloc, you came across what you characterise as check-points. You were still blindfolded at this time, is that right, Mr. Stijovic?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, but there were some groups there that would stop the Ascona and would ask, Who are these people? Why are you letting them go? And some people would curse us. And Nasim then said, Well, these are good guys. We decided we'd let them go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kearney, I have one question. You talked about the tractor that took you from Gllogjan to Dragoslav's place. Who was driving that tractor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know those people from Glodjane. I don't know who it was that drove the tractor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But it was some one of the people that had captured you or belonging to the group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think he was not in the group that had captured us, but I don't know because I hardly knew anyone in the group. So I can't really tell you whether he was in it or not, whether he had participated in this or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Kearney.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: How about the men who were driving the red Ascona car, were they among your initial captors? Who were they, please?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know who drove the car, I don't know the man, but in the front passenger seat of the Ascona there was Nasim - I think it's - Haradinaj, I'm not sure about his last name, but his first name was Nasim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: There was one or two men in the front seat of the Ascona?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Two.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Nasim, the man you mentioned, was he driving or was he the passenger?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kearney, if you read the last question: "I don't know the man, but in the front passenger seat of the Ascona there was Nasim..." Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: I stand corrected. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Were both of those men armed wearing uniform?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember. Nasim was wearing a sweater and camouflage trousers, but for the other two I don't know because my -- I was blindfolded, and they didn't even get out of the car at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: When you say "the other two," were there two other men in the car besides Nasim and yourself and your cousins or -- please tell us exactly what you mean?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Nasim, the driver, and the three of us in the back seat all tied up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: When you were taken to a -- you said you were taken to an area near Babaloc. You were taken out of the car, and you were blindfolded, and the ties to your hands were taken off at that point. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Were there -- at the point where you were untied, were there KLA soldiers there?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Where? When they untied our hands? The two that took us there untied our hands. We were not supposed to look around or to look back. We were supposed to look straight ahead, so I don't know whether there were any KLA soldiers there apart from the two of them that had actually brought us to that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: The two soldiers at this point, Nasim and the other gentleman, did they have their weapons drawn at this point when you were being untied? Were the weapons out and pointed at you, or were they -- they holstered somehow?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: When they untied our hands, their weapons were drawn, and they told us to walk straight and not to look back because otherwise they'd kill us or shoot us. That's what they meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And did you do that? Did you walk away from them at that point?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. We walked. We didn't dare look -- to look back. First, the three of us went together, and then after a while I stayed back with Dragoslav to help him, and Mijat, Kika, ran to the refugee camp and asked a man with a car to drive us to the hospital in Decani, to the infirmary in Decani.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: This is the -- this is a refugee camp, where? Was it in Babaloc, Mr. Stijovic?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, in Babaloc.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: From the point where you were released until you actually arrived into Babaloc, how far was that? How far outside of Babaloc were you released?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, about 500 metres from the camp, maybe a little bit more or a little bit less, but something like that, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And this refugee camp you're referring to, this was a refugee camp for Serbs, I presume? Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: For Serbs from Albania, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: At that time, was the village of Babaloc a Serb-controlled area, if you know?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand your question. What do you mean Serb-controlled? This was where Serbs who had fled from Albania had their accommodation. This is what had been set up for them, and mostly these people were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: When you arrived at the area of the refugee camp, did you see any either Serb police or Serb soldiers at that time?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: How about any more KLA soldiers, did you see any more KLA soldiers in that area in Babaloc in the refugee camp?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: In the refugee camp in Babaloc, the Serbs who you are talking about who had fled from Albania, were they allowed to move around freely? Were they prisoners there? Were they under guard of someone or were they just living there?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Where, in Babaloc.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: They were living there, that's where their homes were. They were moving around.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: You indicated at some point after this, on this day, you went to receive medical treatment. Can you tell us more about that, please?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: First we were admitted to the out-patient clinic in Decani, where we were administered first aid and then they told us to go to the Pec hospital. We went there and they took X-rays of Dragoslav's injuries and put him on the first ambulance to Pristina. They told Mijat and me to stay there and receive the hospital treatment, which I refused and so did Mijat for reasons of our own personal safety. I felt more comfortable being at home among my own people, my family. I was too scared to stay there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Can you describe the physical injuries you suffered during this day of beating for us, please?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: I had cuts on my head, gashes on my ear, all over my head. My back was covered in bruises, my rump from the clubs and the blows that they dealt us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: How long did you suffer from these injuries after they were inflicted on you?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Over 20 days and more, 20 days and more. I still had the bruises and the shooting pain.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: At some point, Mr. Stijovic, did you actually leave Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: I left Kosovo in June 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Why did you leave?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Why did I leave? I left because I was too scared to stay. The way I'd fared the first time around, I certainly never wished for anything like that to happen to me again or worse.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: When you left Kosovo, did you leave any of your personal property behind?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: All that I had was left behind. I had a house in Dasinovac, a stable, 4 acres [as interpreted] and 75 ares of land and it all remained in Dasinovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: After your beating and your release, did you ever actually try to go back to your land in Dasinovac?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kearney. Mr. Emmerson, I'm just wondering whether it would be --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- better to have a break now or --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: There's one minor technical matter I need to attend to, before I cross-examine in any event. If Your Honours were to resume by half past 12.00, I'm confident that I could complete the cross-examination of this witness before the end of the next session and leave time for any re-examination as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is there any need as far as you've heard now, Mr. Guy-Smith or Mr. Harvey?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If any questions were to be asked, they would be three in number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Certainly not more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I suggest that we first ask Madam Usher to escort the witness out of the courtroom. We have a break, and we'll resume in approximately 20 minutes, Mr. Stijovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, just a scheduling matter. Did the Chamber -- Trial Chambers receive communication from the Office of the Prosecutor about scheduling for today? We -- even though we had other witnesses --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we've received that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There's one other matter before I give you an opportunity to raise any matters, Mr. Emmerson. There is an issue about the Chamber having requested the Prosecution to provide us with material in relation to, I would say, general security situation in Kosovo. We also do understand that the Prosecution has some fear that such material might be -- the Defence might -- that this material might be contaminated by matters which might not be favourable to the accused, and therefore the suggestion is, as I understand, to present to the Chamber stipulated facts on the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can I just respond briefly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The position is this: The material that Your Honour's requested and there's other material, too, is highly variable in quality. Some of it has already been presented to the Trial Chamber and the Appeals Chamber in the course of provisional release applications, and in each instance findings have been made that there was no basis certainly so far as my client was concerned to draw inferences adverse to him from the material. But there are a number of issues that it gives rise to, including, first of all, the -- just -- if I may just briefly outline and indicate where we are going.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: First of all, the potential for other evidence to have to be either obtained or adduced; secondly the appropriate form by which that type of material is properly to be introduced; and thirdly, to what issues does it properly go. I had an opportunity to speak briefly with a member of the Trial Chamber staff, who indicated to me that the Trial Chamber's interest was in respect of the third of the criteria outlined for witness protection measures in respect of those witnesses who had not received threats themselves; that criterion being the criterion that there would be an unstable situation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the third criteria is there exists an unstable security situation in that territory, which is particularly unfavourable to witnesses who appear before the Tribunal. That's the criteria.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, can I respond in this way at this point. The appropriate approach is a matter which is actively under discussion amongst the Defence teams and, of course, would be the subject of discussion with our clients. One option, and it's an option that I think we've pursued in all cases, save one, thus far, is that the Defence have not and do not object to protective measures in respect of any witness who requests them, providing the second criterion is properly established; in other words, and -- and the first, of course. In other words, that the evidence is such that it may antagonise; and, secondly, that the witness has a proper connection to Kosovo. That has been our position thus far, and I have no reason to suppose it will change. The only witness in respect of whom we've raised any issue in that regard was the late request for protective measures for Stanisa Radosevic, which were not granted because they were essentially based on criteria that didn't fulfil the first or the second of the two limbs. So that much, I think, is clear at this stage. There are active discussions amongst the Defence and in due course between the parties about the possibility of stipulation if that is necessary, but it may well be it doesn't need to reach that point if there is no objection from the Defence in respect of protective measures which, as I say, has been the position in any event hitherto. What we're anxious to avoid is satellite litigation on the meaning of this material, appropriate inferences in the ways in which it is to be introduced and tested if it's to be part of a formal decision-making process by the Trial Chamber. So that -- I'm sorry for that rather lengthy short explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear to the Chamber. Mr. Di Fazio and Mr. Kearney, the term "satellite litigation" is new for me, but it clearly expresses what might become a concern if we have to litigate in full detail on all kind of matters just in order to be able to apply the third part of the test I just read. Mr. Di Fazio, is the -- I mean, if both parties would agree that that situation does exist in general terms, of course it could be that once you would say, well, exception should be made for this and this witness where the situation is totally different from what in general terms exists in the area. But is the Prosecution willing to see whether they can reach an agreement and to make a common stipulation to the Chamber, so that we don't have -- so that we don't have to spend a lot of time on considering whether or not the third element of the test would be met. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, both Mr. Kearney and myself are in a bit of a vacuum concerning this issue; however, one thing I do feel confident about is that the Prosecution would be willing to see whether we can reach an agreement. I'm certain -- I'm certain of that. And I'm sure that we can at least initiate discussions to see if there's possibility of that bearing fruit --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I had, in fact, already raised it with Mr. Re --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and I take it then that the Prosecution will not file any material up till the moment that these conversations have been concluded? MR. DI FAZIO: I'm certain that that would be the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Therefore, the Chamber would like to be informed if no agreement could be reached, because then the Chamber, of course, would have to consider what would be the appropriate way of filing any material. Yes, thank you. Any other matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we adjourn until 25 minutes to 1.00, that would still be sufficient?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We need 20 minutes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before I give you an opportunity to cross-examine the witness, Mr. Emmerson, I've got one question for Mr. Kearney. Mr. Kearney, there was one question you introduced by - let me just find it - by saying -- you said something like, You mentioned Mr. Lekaj. And I couldn't find where the witness mentioned that in his testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: It was there earlier, Your Honour. He had -- he was getting -- giving a narrative-type answer. He had mentioned a person he knew, having met in the corridor outside the room, named Lekaj and then I came back to it later in the testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the first time I couldn't --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: That was Deli, I believe, D-e-l-i.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: The first time the name is misspelled as J-e-k-a-j. This is page 56, line 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. Thank you very much. Mr. Emmerson, please proceed. Mr. Stijovic, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Emmerson, who is counsel for Mr. Haradinaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Will Your Honour just give me one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Mr. Stijovic, before I start, I want to make sure that you fully understand the questions that you're being asked in a language that you understand. You're nodding. You've understood clearly the questions you've been asked by Mr. Kearney, for example?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You had no problem understanding what it was he was asking you through the translation?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And, in particular, you understood the questions he asked you when he first stood up --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'll just wait a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: In particular, you understood the questions that he asked you when he first stood up about your employment?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No difficulty with understanding what he was asking you?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can I just ask you for one matter of clarification, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Could we have on the screen Defence document identification 1D0040029, and in the B/C/S version it's a different number, because it's not linked at the moment, which is 1D0040038. They are linked, apparently.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Stijovic, can we just look towards the bottom and check that that is your signature. I think your signature appears --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Perhaps the witness could just briefly be shown the English, first of all, the first page of the English statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Do you see at the bottom there, is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can we again go back to the B/C/S version for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: This is a translation into your own language of the statement that you made to the Prosecution on the 28th of May, 2002. Do you see that? You can see the details there with your name and so forth. Can we just look down, please, a little further on the screen under the line there, just immediately beneath the line. On the right-hand side, it records that your former occupation was that of carpenter. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the furniture factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. And your current occupation in May 2002 is described as a receptionist with the VJ. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: A contractor in the VJ, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: As of 2002, a soldier contractor in the VJ -- as of 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: What is a soldier contractor in the VJ? What does it mean?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: I have a contract. I control some construction equipment. If you don't turn in a satisfactory performance after a year, your contract is terminated. That's what it means.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I understand. You said a soldier contractor. What does that mean, a soldier contractor?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: What do I mean when I say that?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: As of 2000, I have been working as a soldier contractor with the army. I oversee their construction equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And do you have a rank?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your answer, Mr. Stijovic, about your rank.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Lance-corporal.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And when did you first become an employee or contractor, lance-corporal contractor for the VJ?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: On the 3rd of April, 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I want to ask you about a question and answer that you gave in answer to Mr. Kearney. You may remember I asked you just a few moments ago: Did you fully understand the questions that you were being asked? And you told us that you did --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And this is for Your Honours line 39 -- sorry, page 39, it's the very end of page 38, line 25?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm going to read this to you slowly, Mr. Stijovic, so that you understand what it is you were asked and what you told us on oath. Mr. Kearney asked you this: "Tell us, please, today how you are employed first of all?" And you answered: "I am a construction machinery operator now. "Q. During the course of your employment career, did you ever work for the VJ, please?" And you answered: "No." Could you tell us why that was, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm going to -- I'm sorry, Mr. Stijovic. I'm going to ask that Mr. Emmerson then ask the following question in that sequence. I think it -- without the follow-up question --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No, no, I'm --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: -- that clarifies the earlier question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kearney we -- could you please answer the question put to you by Mr. Emmerson. Mr. Emmerson asked you when you said: "No" to a question whether you ever worked for the VJ why you did answer in that way, why you just told Mr. Emmerson that you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Up until 2000 I had never been employed by the Yugoslav Army. That's how I understood the question. As of 2000, I got a job with the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The question, Mr. Stijovic --

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I misunderstood the question the first time around. I meant it was in reference to the time between 1997 and 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'll come back to that, because I asked you just a moment ago when I first stood up whether you had fully understood Mr. Kearney's questions to you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the same time, Mr. Emmerson, if you look at page 38, line 23, you'll see that a certain time-frame is introduced there. The point is clear you make at this moment. I don't know whether to what extent you want to pursue the matter but I leave it to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can I pursue it the way Mr. Kearney just asked me to because it was clarified with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: After you had told us, on oath, that you were never employed by the VJ, Mr. Stijovic, you were then asked: "Were you ever in the army, sir?" And you say: "I was in the army. "Q. What dates were you in the army? "A. 1991 and 1992." Mr. Stijovic, why didn't you tell the Trial Chamber that you were a lance-corporal in the VJ from 2000 until today?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question. I was talking about 1997, 1998, and 1999. I didn't understand the question to be in reference to the period after 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Mr. Stijovic, you were asked again very clearly: "Were you ever in the army?" And you replied that you were, not in 1998 but in 1991 and 1992. Now, why was it that you didn't say to the Tribunal: I was in the army in 1991 and 1992, and since 2000 and to date I've been a lance-corporal? Why didn't you tell the Trial Chamber that?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: I thought we were talking about the period up to 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see. Has anybody suggested to you, Mr. Stijovic, that it would be a good idea if you and your cousins concealed the involvement of yourself and other members of your family in the VJ or the police?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Let me ask you this then: Predrag Stojanovic, he was a police officer in 1998, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Predrag Stojanovic, you mean Dragan? I know him as Dragan.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very well. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that the same?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Is Dragan another name for Predrag?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: It's possible, it's possible. I know him as Dragan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but isn't the witness referring to Dragoslav at this moment? That's what -- when you're talking about Drag --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not Dragoslav, Dragan. That's what we called him, Dragan. I'm not quite sure that his real name is actually Predrag.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Let's just be clear. Dragoslav's nickname is Drago, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Dragoslav?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: His nickname is Drago, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know of that nickname.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see. Let's just go through the brothers briefly. There's Mijat you've told us about; you knew him?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: There is Dragoslav you've told us about; you knew him?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: There's a brother called Veselin, is that right, or Vesko?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And can you tell us the remainder, please, the other two brothers' names?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Vlado and Dragan, could be Predrag. I'm not sure. I know him as Dragan.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, answer the next question very carefully, Mr. Stijovic, and search your memory and so there's no misunderstanding. I'm not asking you about any particular time-period. As far as you know, apart from Dragan, were any of the other brothers ever involved in the police or the army in any way?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Not that I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And you yourself were not in the police reserve at any time?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see. Can I ask you then again by reference to some of the evidence that you've already given to us, you told us about the incident when the armed men came into the Stojanovics' house on the 18th of April, beat Dragoslav, and then beat you and Mijat. That's the part of your evidence I want to ask you about. And you were asked whether you learnt the names of any of those men from either Dragoslav or Mijat, and you gave us two names. You told us that they gave you the name of Nasim, and you described him as the person who tried to protect us.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And that's the man you've described as Nasim Haradinaj, is it?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: I think he's a Haradinaj, but I'm not sure about his surname.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: This is the way the witness put it also last time.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And what did he do to try to protect you?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: He was pushing the soldiers away from us and trying to keep them from beating us.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Was he saying anything to them?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: He was, but I didn't understand what.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see. But it was clear to you he was trying to stop them beating you?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was pushing them away from us.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, in your witness statement I'm going to read to you a sentence that appears there, with your signature on the same page. I'll read it slowly to you. You said: "I think that Nasim was in charge of the soldiers at my cousins' house, as he was the one who eventually ordered the others to stop beating us, and he was also the one who gave us -- who gave orders for us to be taken outside."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just state for a moment in the future if Mr. Emmerson refers to a particular part of a statement, just for ease of the Prosecutor to find that statement, could we know what year the statement was and what page it was taken from, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I've already taken the witness to the statement, identified his signature, and given the date of the 28th of May, 2002.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it Mr. Kearney is asking where to find it in the statement, so for us to be later to --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Page 3 of the text, paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'll ask the question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You said in your witness statement: "I think Nasim was in charge of the soldiers at my cousins' house, as he was the one who eventually ordered the others to stop beating us, and he was also the one who gave orders for us to be taken outside." Does that accord with your recollection?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: I said I think he was one of the most influential people there. I didn't say "in charge." It may have been a mistranslation. I said one of the most influential people wielding the most influence in that group. It could have been a mistranslation. I never said he was in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Was there somebody else there who seemed to be in charge, above him?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see. But despite having this influence, he wasn't able to stop the other people from beating you?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: It was only for brief moments, but then he left and they continued to beat us.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So did they stop when he told them to stop and tried to pull them away?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: He was pushing them from us, pushing them away, fending them off. Those were whole groups of people beating us, and he would push one group at a time in a bid to protect us.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: But despite the fact that he seemed to you to be the person with influence, he wasn't able to stop this from happening?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: For as long as he was there, he was quite successful, but he didn't stay for long enough to entirely protect us from the beatings.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So it was only when he left that the beatings continued?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, as soon as he left, they would beat us again.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, you gave us another name that you had been told by Mijat and Dragoslav who you described as the person who had beaten you in the small room, and the name I think you gave us was Zeqir Nimonaj, is that correct, or just Zeqir perhaps?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Zeqir, Zeqir.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, looking at your witness statement, and it's the same paragraph as I was referring to before, you say this: "I can only recall the names of two of these soldiers who were familiar with Dragoslav. These were the men with the first names Nasim and Zeqir."

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And those were the names that Dragoslav and Mijat gave you, were they?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I memorised those two names. There were other names being dropped, but I did not memorise any. I remembered Nasim because he was the one who tried to protect us, and I remembered Zeqir because he was the one who administered the most severe beatings.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: But you don't remember any other specific names that they gave you?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't. I wasn't asking about the names because I didn't know any of the people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You don't, for example, remember them telling you that Daut Haradinaj was amongst the men in the room?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Daut Haradinaj? I didn't comment on those issues with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So they never mentioned that to you, is that correct, they never mentioned that name to you?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't discuss this. They did mention some names. They did mention Daut, yes, but I couldn't remember that when I was giving my statement. I don't know who that man is.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see. So you've given your evidence-in-chief, you've given your witness statement, and you're now recalling, are you, that they did mention the name Daut to you? Is that the truth, Mr. Stijovic?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: That they mentioned Daut's name to me?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Is that the truth? Because a few moments ago, you told us you couldn't remember any others.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: I heard the name Daut, but - how can I explain to you? When they beat us, those were the two names that stuck in my mind. That's what I put in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And certainly the one who stuck in your mind as the most influential and who you described as being in charge in your statement was Nasim?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: To my mind, yes, in my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, you told us that as you were walking along the road or being walked along the road to -- towards Gllogjan, you were told to put your hands in the air, to keep your heads down, and not to look left or right. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And is that an instruction that was given to all three of you?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And as far as you could see, were all three of you walking along with your arms in the air?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, from time to time, yes, we were trying to assist Dragoslav a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And I think you said that you and Mijat were in a great deal of pain and bleeding as you were walking along. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was bleeding and so was Dragoslav.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: What about Mijat?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Mijat, I don't remember about him but I and Dragoslav, we were all covered in blood. I know that later on when we had to wash ourselves at the pump, only the two of us were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And as far as you could tell, did the other two obey the instruction to keep their heads down and not to look left or right as you were walking along?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, I just want to go back to some of the incidents that you described as having caused you to leave Dashinoc -- Dasinovac in the first place?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You listed for us a number of incidents and I just want to make sure I've understood them correctly because I'm not sure the transcript correctly recorded what you were saying. You told us that you had read about an attack on somebody's house in the paper, that you knew the people concerned, and that you went to speak to them. Can you tell us the name, the family name, of the people that that incident concerned?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that was Malesa Culafic's house in Donji Ratis, and we were actually family friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Malesa Culafic, C-u-l-a-f-i-c?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Were you aware of a property dispute between your friends, the Culafics, and somebody else who lived nearby, a dispute about the ownership of some land?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that, but I don't believe that because these were elderly people. They'd lived there in Ratis since the day they were born.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see. You mentioned an attack on Irzniq police station. I think you told us that you read about that but didn't see the evidence for your -- for yourself. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, yes, I read about it in the papers and I saw it on TV. They covered this incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Then the third thing you listed for us was what you described as the murder of a police officer called Otovic. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And that was something that had happened on the 24th of March, right outside your cousins' house, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: As far as they told me, it was right next to their house.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And then the last thing you mentioned was that people would pass by at night firing shots. Did you ever see that or hear it yourself?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, gun-fire and that kind of thing, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, that's a different question. Let me pull it apart into stages. You heard the sounds of gun-fire from your home in Dashinoc?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, gun-fire, automatic rifles. As they walked down the road they discharged their weapons in order to scare the people. That's what I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, just be clear what you yourself heard or saw. When, on how many occasions, did you hear gun-fire?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: How many times? Well, it would happen often, especially at night, I mean after nightfall.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And where exactly did you hear the gun-fire?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in my village next to the houses, there was the main road that passed by our houses and as they -- as the cars drove by people would discharge their weapons in order to intimidate people.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see. And how -- when exactly did those incidents occur?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Just before we left the village, our house in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, you've told us you left your house in the village at the end of March; correct?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't say in late March. I said sometime in March or April. I didn't know the exact date, so it's late March or April.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, I think just to be absolutely clear, what you said was sometime in late March or early April. That was after, I think, the --

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I haven't finished the question. That was after the killing of Otovic, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So the gun-fire that you started to hear all took place after the incident in Gllogjan on the 24th of March. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the gun-fire that was heard before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, I'm sorry. To be absolutely clear about your answer --

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: What -- I just didn't understand your question. Could you please repeat it?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, I'm looking --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, let me just try to find out. Did you hear this fire at night in your village also before Otovic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Dasinovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, in Dasinovac, did you hear that also before Otovic was killed or only after Otovic was killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before and after the killing of Otovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You told us in your evidence in chief a little while ago when asked by Mr. Kearney to describe the hatred, as you put it, that you could pick up from the people in Gllogjan on the 18th of April, you said: "There could be no reason for it, apart from the fact that we were Serbs. There could not be any other reason. I have never clashed with them and neither had Mijat, as far as I know." Is that a fair summary of your evidence?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: You mean for myself? I didn't mention Mijat or Dragoslav. They hit us because we were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, you did, in fact, mention Mijat, but never mind that for the moment. Is it your evidence that you had no idea why the people of Gllogjan village might be attacking Mijat and Dragoslav Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Had they told you about what happened on the 24th of March in Gllogjan?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: In Glodjane on the 24th of March?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Had your cousins told you what happened in Gllogjan on the 24th of March?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Had you discussed with Dragoslav and Mijat what had happened on the day that Otovic was killed?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: When Otovic was killed? Well, they just told me that they had left their house that night for safety reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Did they not tell you that their house had been used as a position from which to fire by the police on the Haradinaj compound? Did they not tell you that?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: No. This is the first time that I hear of something like that. We didn't discuss this at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
